pack.description: Functional language: connectors, hedging, agreement and disagreement, signposts for spoken answers, and email formulas for requests, complaints, apologies, follow-ups and recommendations.
pack.selection_note: Internal high-yield selection of connectors and formulas for the Email, Academic Discussion and Interview tasks; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: for the reason that has just been given
entries.example_academic: The sample was small; the results should therefore be interpreted with caution.
entries.example_spoken: I missed the bus and therefore got to class late.

entries.definition: used to introduce what happened because of the thing just mentioned
entries.example_academic: Rainfall declined for a decade; as a result, harvests fell by a third.
entries.example_spoken: I stayed up all night and, as a result, I slept through my alarm.

entries.definition: because of something
entries.translation_fr: en raison de, à cause de
entries.example_academic: The delay was due to a shortage of qualified engineers.
entries.example_spoken: The game was cancelled due to rain.

entries.definition: used to give the reason for something
entries.example_academic: Many species have disappeared because of habitat loss.
entries.example_spoken: I was late because of the traffic.

entries.definition: to cause something to happen or exist
entries.example_academic: Overuse of antibiotics can lead to resistant strains of bacteria.
entries.example_spoken: Skipping breakfast always leads to a bad morning for me.

entries.definition: as a result of what has just been said
entries.example_academic: Funding was withdrawn, and consequently the project was abandoned.
entries.example_spoken: My laptop broke and, consequently, I lost half my notes.

entries.definition: as a result of this; or in this way
entries.example_academic: The two groups never met and thus developed separate dialects.
entries.example_spoken: He practiced every day and thus improved quickly.

entries.definition: for this reason; used to introduce a result or an explanation of a name
entries.example_academic: The metal expands when heated; hence the gaps left between the rails.
entries.example_spoken: The café is in an old bank, hence the name "The Vault."

entries.definition: to be caused by something; to have something as its origin
entries.example_academic: Many of the errors stem from a misunderstanding of the original text.
entries.example_spoken: Most of our arguments stem from who does the dishes.

entries.definition: to cause something to happen or exist
entries.example_academic: The discovery gave rise to an entirely new field of research.
entries.example_spoken: That rule change gave rise to a lot of complaints.

entries.definition: happening after and often because of an important event
entries.translation_fr: à la suite de, dans le sillage de
entries.example_academic: In the wake of the crisis, regulators tightened the rules on lending.
entries.example_spoken: In the wake of the scandal, the coach resigned.

entries.definition: used to introduce a fact that makes the main statement surprising
entries.example_academic: Although the method is expensive, it yields far more reliable data.
entries.example_spoken: Although I studied a lot, I found the exam hard.

entries.definition: used to introduce a statement that contrasts with what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The theory is elegant; however, it has never been tested.
entries.example_spoken: I like the course. However, the workload is heavy.

entries.definition: used to stress that something is true in spite of the fact that follows
entries.example_academic: Even though emissions fell, concentrations in the atmosphere continued to rise.
entries.example_spoken: I went to class even though I had a cold.

entries.definition: without being prevented or affected by something
entries.example_academic: Despite its small size, the country exports a wide range of goods.
entries.example_spoken: We had a good time despite the weather.

entries.definition: used to introduce a different or opposite point of view
entries.example_academic: Nuclear power produces little carbon; on the other hand, its waste remains dangerous for centuries.
entries.example_spoken: The apartment is cheap. On the other hand, it's far from campus.

entries.definition: in spite of what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The evidence is incomplete; nevertheless, a pattern is beginning to emerge.
entries.example_spoken: It was raining; nevertheless, we went for a run.

entries.definition: used to compare two facts and show that they are different
entries.example_academic: Mammals regulate their body temperature, whereas reptiles depend on external heat.
entries.example_spoken: I like mornings, whereas my roommate works best at night.

entries.definition: used to contrast two facts, or to admit one point before making another
entries.example_academic: While the reform reduced costs, it also lowered the quality of service.
entries.example_spoken: While I see the advantages, I still prefer the old system.

entries.definition: in spite of what has just been mentioned
entries.example_academic: The task was difficult; the team nonetheless completed it on time.
entries.example_spoken: It's a small improvement, but nonetheless it's progress.

entries.definition: used to add information that slightly reduces the force of what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The economy continued to grow, albeit at a slower pace.
entries.example_spoken: I finished the essay, albeit two hours late.

entries.definition: used before adding a point that limits or contrasts with what you have just stated
entries.example_academic: The survey has clear weaknesses. That said, it remains the best source available.
entries.example_spoken: The class is tough. That said, I'm learning a lot.

entries.definition: without being affected by something; in spite of
entries.example_academic: Notwithstanding these limitations, the study makes an important contribution.
entries.example_spoken: Notwithstanding the rain, the ceremony went ahead outside.

entries.definition: used to accept that something may be true before saying it does not change your view
entries.example_academic: Costs have certainly risen. Be that as it may, the investment remains justified.
entries.example_spoken: You say he's busy. Be that as it may, he should have answered.

entries.definition: partly, but not completely
entries.example_academic: The decline can be explained, to some extent, by changes in diet.
entries.example_spoken: To some extent, I think the professor is right.

entries.definition: usually, though not always
entries.example_academic: In most cases, the infection clears without treatment.
entries.example_spoken: In most cases, I just email the professor directly.

entries.definition: used to say that something will probably happen or is probably true
entries.example_academic: It is likely that the tools were made elsewhere and brought to the site.
entries.example_spoken: It is likely that the exam will be moved to Friday.

entries.definition: used to say that something is true in most situations
entries.example_academic: Generally speaking, larger firms invest more in training.
entries.example_spoken: Generally speaking, I prefer working in a group.

entries.definition: used when giving an opinion that you believe could be supported with good reasons
entries.translation_fr: sans doute, on peut soutenir que
entries.example_academic: This is arguably the most influential experiment in the history of the field.
entries.example_spoken: It's arguably the best café near campus.

entries.definition: used to say what you think is probably true although you are not certain
entries.example_academic: The settlement was abandoned, presumably because the wells ran dry.
entries.example_spoken: Presumably she got my message, since she showed up.

entries.definition: used to introduce a view that is reasonable but that you do not state as certain
entries.example_academic: It could be argued that the reform simply moved the problem elsewhere.
entries.example_spoken: It could be argued that group work wastes more time than it saves.

entries.definition: used to say that something is very probably true or will very probably happen
entries.example_academic: In all likelihood, the manuscript was copied in a northern monastery.
entries.example_spoken: In all likelihood, they'll cancel the Friday session.

entries.definition: in general; when everything is considered
entries.example_academic: By and large, the predictions of the model have been confirmed.
entries.example_spoken: By and large, I'm happy with my schedule.

entries.definition: to the degree that
entries.example_academic: The policy succeeded insofar as it reduced unemployment among the young.
entries.example_spoken: I'll help insofar as my schedule allows.

entries.definition: used to add a warning or limit to what you have just said
entries.example_academic: The results are encouraging, with the caveat that the sample was small.
entries.example_spoken: I recommend the course, with the caveat that it takes a lot of time.

entries.definition: used to say that you understand someone's opinion, often before disagreeing in part
entries.translation_fr: je vois ce que vous voulez dire
entries.example_academic: I see your point about cost; my concern, however, is with safety.
entries.example_spoken: I see your point, but I still think we should start earlier.

entries.definition: used to accept that what someone has said is reasonable
entries.example_academic: That's a fair point, and the revised draft now addresses it directly.
entries.example_spoken: That's a fair point; I hadn't thought about the cost.

entries.definition: a polite way of saying that you doubt or disagree with something
entries.translation_fr: je n'en suis pas si sûr
entries.example_academic: I'm not sure about that; the figures in the second table suggest the opposite.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not sure about that. Didn't the professor say Thursday?

entries.definition: used to say that you understand what someone is trying to say
entries.translation_fr: je vois ce que tu veux dire
entries.example_academic: I see what you mean, although the author's definition is narrower than yours.
entries.example_spoken: Oh, I see what you mean: the two graphs don't match.

entries.definition: used to say that you agree completely
entries.example_academic: I couldn't agree more with the reviewer's comment on the sample size.
entries.example_spoken: I couldn't agree more; that lecture was way too long.

entries.definition: a polite phrase used before disagreeing with or criticizing someone
entries.translation_fr: sauf votre respect, avec tout le respect que je vous dois
entries.example_academic: With all due respect, the committee has overlooked a crucial piece of evidence.
entries.example_spoken: With all due respect, I don't think that plan will work.

entries.definition: a polite and rather formal way of saying that you disagree
entries.translation_fr: permettez-moi de ne pas être d'accord
entries.example_academic: The author claims the question is settled; I beg to differ.
entries.example_spoken: You think the test was easy? I beg to differ.

entries.definition: used to say that you mostly agree, without being completely certain
entries.example_academic: I'm inclined to agree with the second reviewer that the title is misleading.
entries.example_spoken: I'm inclined to agree with you, but let's hear what Sam thinks.

entries.definition: to agree with someone or have the same opinion
entries.translation_fr: être du même avis, souscrire à
entries.example_academic: Most specialists concur that the document is a later forgery.
entries.example_spoken: I concur with everything she just said.

entries.definition: to disagree with something that someone has said or done
entries.example_academic: Several historians take issue with this reading of the sources.
entries.example_spoken: I take issue with the idea that we didn't work hard enough.

entries.definition: used to introduce the first of several points
entries.example_academic: First of all, the study defines what it means by poverty.
entries.example_spoken: First of all, I'd like to thank everyone for coming.

entries.definition: used to introduce an example
entries.example_academic: Some metals, for instance copper, conduct heat extremely well.
entries.example_spoken: You could, for instance, record yourself and listen back.

entries.definition: used to show that what follows is what you think
entries.example_academic: In my opinion, the second explanation accounts for more of the evidence.
entries.example_spoken: In my opinion, online classes work better for big lectures.

entries.definition: used to say something again in a simpler or clearer way
entries.example_academic: The gene is recessive; in other words, both parents must carry it.
entries.example_spoken: He never replied. In other words, we're on our own.

entries.definition: used to explain more clearly something you have just said
entries.translation_fr: ce que je veux dire, c'est que
entries.example_academic: What I mean is that the two processes cannot be studied separately.
entries.example_spoken: What I mean is, we should split the work more fairly.

entries.definition: in addition to what has just been mentioned
entries.translation_fr: en plus de cela, par-dessus le marché
entries.example_academic: Yields were poor, and on top of that, transport costs doubled.
entries.example_spoken: I have two essays due and, on top of that, a shift on Saturday.

entries.definition: used to introduce a short statement of the main points
entries.example_academic: To sum up, the evidence favors the second hypothesis.
entries.example_spoken: To sum up, I think living on campus is worth the cost.

entries.definition: used to add another fact or point
entries.example_academic: In addition, the survey recorded the age and occupation of each respondent.
entries.example_spoken: In addition, we'd need someone to book the room.

entries.definition: used to add information that supports what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The method is cheap; moreover, it requires no special equipment.
entries.example_spoken: The room is too small and, moreover, it has no projector.

entries.definition: used to say that you think something is true but you are not completely sure
entries.example_academic: As far as I know, no comparable study has been carried out.
entries.example_spoken: As far as I know, the library closes at ten.

entries.definition: used to give your personal opinion about something
entries.example_academic: As far as I'm concerned, the second proposal is the stronger of the two.
entries.example_spoken: As far as I'm concerned, we can meet any day but Friday.

entries.definition: in addition to what has just been stated
entries.example_academic: The data are incomplete; furthermore, they were collected by different methods.
entries.example_spoken: It's expensive and, furthermore, it's a long way from campus.

entries.definition: used before explaining something again in different words
entries.translation_fr: autrement dit, pour le dire autrement
entries.example_academic: To put it another way, growth without investment cannot last.
entries.example_spoken: To put it another way, we have three days and ten chapters.

entries.definition: concerning a particular subject
entries.translation_fr: en ce qui concerne, quant à
entries.example_academic: With regard to funding, the report recommends no immediate change.
entries.example_spoken: With regard to your question, I'll check and get back to you.

entries.definition: used to give a judgment after thinking about every part of a situation
entries.example_academic: All things considered, the benefits of the program outweigh its costs.
entries.example_spoken: All things considered, the presentation went pretty well.

entries.definition: used to say that you will give only the main point and no more detail
entries.example_academic: Suffice it to say that the two accounts cannot both be accurate.
entries.example_spoken: Suffice it to say, the group meeting did not go well.

entries.definition: a standard way of beginning a formal email by stating why you are sending it
entries.example_academic: I am writing to request an extension for the research proposal.
entries.example_spoken: I started with "I am writing to ask about my application"; is that too formal?

entries.definition: a polite way of asking someone to do something
entries.example_academic: Could you please confirm whether the seminar room is available on Tuesday?
entries.example_spoken: Could you please send me the slides after class?

entries.definition: a polite way of asking for something by saying you would be thankful for it
entries.translation_fr: je vous serais reconnaissant de bien vouloir
entries.example_academic: I would appreciate it if you could send me the reading list in advance.
entries.example_spoken: I would really appreciate it if you could look at my draft.

entries.definition: a soft, polite way of introducing a request or question
entries.example_academic: I was wondering if it would be possible to reschedule our meeting.
entries.example_spoken: I was wondering if you could lend me your notes.

entries.definition: a polite way of asking whether something can be done
entries.example_academic: Would it be possible to submit the form by post rather than online?
entries.example_spoken: Would it be possible to move my shift to Sunday?

entries.definition: a formal and polite way of asking someone to do something
entries.example_academic: I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this application.
entries.example_spoken: I ended the email with "I would be grateful if you could reply by Friday."

entries.definition: as soon as you are able to, without being rushed
entries.translation_fr: dès que cela vous sera possible
entries.example_academic: Please return the signed form at your earliest convenience.
entries.example_spoken: She told me to call back at your earliest convenience, which sounded very official.

entries.headword: should you need any further information
entries.definition: a formal way of offering to give more details if the reader wants them
entries.translation_fr: si vous avez besoin de renseignements complémentaires
entries.example_academic: Should you need any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me.
entries.example_spoken: I closed with "Should you need any further information, I'm happy to help."

entries.headword: I would be much obliged if
entries.definition: a very formal way of asking for something, expressing thanks in advance
entries.translation_fr: je vous serais très obligé de
entries.example_academic: I would be much obliged if you could forward this request to the committee.
entries.example_spoken: My grandfather still writes "I would be much obliged if you could reply."
synonyms: I would be most grateful if

entries.definition: used to say that something is sad, disappointing or has a bad effect
entries.example_academic: Unfortunately, the heating in the apartment has not worked since Monday.
entries.example_spoken: Unfortunately, I can't make it to the meeting.

entries.definition: used to tell someone that a result or service was worse than you expected
entries.example_academic: I am disappointed that my earlier message has not received a reply.
entries.example_spoken: I am disappointed that nobody told us about the change.

entries.definition: used in a formal message to say that you are worried about a situation
entries.translation_fr: faire part de mon inquiétude au sujet de
entries.example_academic: I am writing to express my concern about the noise from the construction site.
entries.example_spoken: I wanted to express my concern about how the groups were chosen.

entries.definition: to fail to reach a standard or level that was expected
entries.translation_fr: ne pas être à la hauteur de
entries.example_academic: The quality of the accommodation fell short of what was advertised.
entries.example_spoken: The workshop fell short of my expectations.

entries.definition: used to say that something made you feel shocked and disappointed
entries.example_academic: To my dismay, the order arrived three weeks late and incomplete.
entries.example_spoken: To my dismay, the printer broke an hour before the deadline.

entries.definition: to correct something that is wrong
entries.example_academic: I trust that you will take steps to rectify the situation promptly.
entries.example_spoken: They promised to rectify the mistake on my bill.

entries.headword: leave a great deal to be desired
entries.definition: to be much worse than it should be
entries.example_academic: The cleanliness of the shared kitchen leaves a great deal to be desired.
entries.example_spoken: Honestly, the food in that cafeteria leaves a great deal to be desired.
entries.ipa: /liːv ə ˈɡreɪt ˌdiːl tə bi dɪˈzaɪərd/

entries.definition: used to say that you are sorry about something you did or caused
entries.translation_fr: je vous prie d'excuser, je m'excuse de
entries.example_academic: I apologize for the delay in replying to your message.
entries.example_spoken: I apologize for being late; my bus broke down.

entries.definition: used to say you regret having caused someone trouble or extra work
entries.example_academic: I am sorry for the inconvenience this change may cause.
entries.example_spoken: Sorry for the inconvenience, but could we meet an hour later?

entries.definition: a formal way of saying that you are sorry
entries.example_academic: Please accept my apologies for missing yesterday's appointment.
entries.example_spoken: I wrote "Please accept my apologies" because I'd forgotten the meeting completely.

entries.headword: I regret to inform you that
entries.definition: a formal way of introducing bad news
entries.translation_fr: j'ai le regret de vous informer que
entries.example_academic: I regret to inform you that I will be unable to attend the conference.
entries.example_spoken: The letter began "I regret to inform you that your application was unsuccessful."

entries.definition: events that nobody expected and that cause a change of plan
entries.example_academic: Due to unforeseen circumstances, the lecture has been postponed until next week.
entries.example_spoken: I had to cancel because of unforeseen circumstances at home.

entries.definition: used to say that you accept that a problem was your fault
entries.example_academic: I take full responsibility for the error in the submitted figures.
entries.example_spoken: I take full responsibility for the mix-up with the room booking.

entries.definition: by accident, without intending to
entries.example_academic: I inadvertently attached an earlier version of the report to my message.
entries.example_spoken: I inadvertently deleted the whole folder.

entries.definition: used to say that you are writing again about something discussed or requested earlier
entries.translation_fr: je reviens vers vous au sujet de
entries.example_academic: I am following up on the request I submitted on the third of March.
entries.example_spoken: I am following up on my email from last week; did you get it?

entries.headword: I look forward to hearing from you
entries.definition: a polite closing line that shows you expect a reply
entries.example_academic: Thank you for your help; I look forward to hearing from you.
entries.example_spoken: I always end with "I look forward to hearing from you."
entries.ipa: /aɪ lʊk ˈfɔːrwərd tə ˌhɪrɪŋ frʌm juː/

entries.definition: a polite way of asking someone to tell you something
entries.example_academic: Please let me know whether Thursday afternoon would be convenient.
entries.example_spoken: Please let me know if you need a ride.

entries.definition: used to refer back to something you have already said or written
entries.example_academic: As I mentioned in my previous message, the form requires your signature.
entries.example_spoken: As I mentioned, I'll be away next week.

entries.definition: used in formal letters and emails to refer to an earlier message or conversation
entries.example_academic: Further to our conversation on Monday, I attach the documents you requested.
entries.example_spoken: He wrote "Further to our call" at the top, which is how they start emails there.

entries.definition: used to say what a formal message is about
entries.translation_fr: au sujet de, en référence à
entries.example_academic: I am writing in reference to the vacancy advertised on your website.
entries.example_spoken: I'm calling in reference to the apartment on Maple Street.

entries.definition: to ask politely how far something, such as an application, has progressed
entries.translation_fr: se renseigner sur l'état d'avancement de
entries.example_academic: I would like to inquire about the status of my scholarship application.
entries.example_spoken: I called to inquire about the status of my refund.

entries.definition: following or according to a rule, agreement or earlier message
entries.example_academic: Pursuant to our agreement of the tenth of May, I enclose the signed contract.
entries.example_spoken: The notice said "pursuant to the housing rules," which just means the rules require it.

entries.definition: used to give advice about what someone should do or choose
entries.example_academic: I would recommend extending the opening hours of the library during examinations.
entries.example_spoken: I would recommend the Tuesday section; the instructor is great.

entries.definition: used to put forward an idea or plan for someone to consider
entries.example_academic: I suggest that the committee postpone the decision until all members are present.
entries.example_spoken: I suggest that we meet at the library instead.

entries.headword: it might be a good idea to
entries.definition: a gentle way of advising someone to do something
entries.translation_fr: ce serait peut-être une bonne idée de
entries.example_academic: It might be a good idea to send a reminder a week before the event.
entries.example_spoken: It might be a good idea to book the room now.
entries.ipa: /ɪt maɪt bi ə ˌɡʊd aɪˈdiːə tuː/

entries.definition: used to offer one possible solution among several
entries.example_academic: One option would be to divide the class into two smaller groups.
entries.example_spoken: One option would be to record the meeting for people who can't come.

entries.definition: used to give firm advice
entries.example_academic: I strongly advise new students to attend the orientation session.
entries.example_spoken: I strongly advise you to start the reading early.

entries.definition: a formal way of saying that doing something is sensible
entries.example_academic: It would be advisable to inform all tenants before the work begins.
entries.example_spoken: It would be advisable to check with your advisor first.

entries.definition: used to advise someone very strongly to do something
entries.example_academic: I would urge you to reconsider the decision to close the reading room.
entries.example_spoken: I would urge you to apply even if you think your grades are too low.

entries.definition: a formal way of saying that an action is careful and sensible given the risks
entries.example_academic: It would be prudent to obtain a second estimate before approving the repairs.
entries.example_spoken: It would be prudent to save a copy before you change anything.

entries.definition: used to say that something appears to be true, although it may not be
entries.example_academic: The seemingly minor change in wording produced a large shift in responses.
entries.example_spoken: It was a seemingly simple question, but nobody could answer it.
entries.example_interview: It was a seemingly simple job, but it taught me more about patience than anything else.
entries.example_discussion: Seemingly minor rules, like dress codes, can shape how students feel about school.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Signals a contrast between appearance and reality. Place it before the adjective: "a seemingly simple task".

entries.definition: used to state a conclusion carefully, as something the evidence suggests rather than proves
entries.example_academic: It would appear that the decline began well before the policy change.
entries.example_spoken: It would appear that someone has already taken the last copy.
entries.example_interview: From what my friends tell me, it would appear that the new schedule suits most people.
entries.example_discussion: It would appear that the policy reduced traffic, although the data cover only one year.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Softer than "it seems that". French speakers often write "it would seem as though that", mixing two structures.

entries.headword: there is some evidence to suggest that
entries.definition: used to present a claim as supported by data but not yet firmly established
entries.example_academic: There is some evidence to suggest that bilingual children switch tasks more easily.
entries.example_spoken: There is some evidence to suggest that naps actually help memory.
entries.ipa: /ðɛr ɪz sʌm ˈɛvədəns tə səˈdʒɛst ðæt/
entries.example_interview: There is some evidence to suggest that music helps concentration, so I study with headphones on.
entries.example_discussion: There is some evidence to suggest that later school start times improve grades, which supports Kim.
entries.usage_note: Formal. A safe way to cite research without overstating it. Do not add "a": "there is some evidence", never "an evidence".

entries.definition: used to say carefully that something is possible, even if it seems unlikely
entries.example_academic: It is not inconceivable that the two populations met before the ice age ended.
entries.example_spoken: It is not inconceivable that the exam gets moved again.
synonyms: it cannot be ruled out that
entries.example_interview: It is not inconceivable that I'll end up teaching, even if it isn't my plan right now.
entries.example_discussion: It is not inconceivable that remote work will reverse the growth of large cities.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Double negative = a cautious "it is possible". Useful to introduce a bold idea without claiming too much.

entries.definition: used to introduce a view that could reasonably be held, without fully committing to it
entries.translation_fr: on pourrait objecter que, on pourrait soutenir que
entries.example_academic: One might argue that the reform simply moved the costs elsewhere.
entries.example_spoken: One might argue that the library should open earlier, not later.
entries.example_interview: One might argue that I spend too much time on sport, but it keeps me focused.
entries.example_discussion: One might argue that the ban is unfair to responsible users, yet the risks are real.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Introduces a view you may or may not share. In speech, "some people would say" is more natural.

entries.definition: partly, but not completely
entries.example_academic: The results support the theory to a certain degree, but several predictions failed.
entries.example_spoken: I agree with you to a certain degree.
entries.example_interview: I agree with that to a certain degree, but my own experience was a bit different.
entries.example_discussion: To a certain degree, Lena is right: price matters, but so does convenience.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Same as "to some extent". French speakers often write "in a certain degree", which is wrong.

entries.definition: when certain aspects are considered, but not all of them
entries.example_academic: In some respects, the two legal systems are remarkably similar.
entries.example_spoken: In some respects, the new dorm is worse than the old one.
entries.example_interview: In some respects, living alone is easier, because I organize my day exactly as I want.
entries.example_discussion: In some respects, the two proposals are similar; both rely on volunteers.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "In some respects", not "in some aspects". Plural "respects" is required.

entries.headword: as far as one can tell
entries.definition: used to say that a statement is based on the limited information available
entries.translation_fr: pour autant qu'on puisse en juger
entries.example_academic: As far as one can tell from the surviving records, the village was abandoned peacefully.
entries.example_spoken: As far as one can tell, the bus isn't coming tonight.
entries.example_interview: As far as one can tell from the reviews, the new café is worth a try.
entries.example_discussion: As far as one can tell from the available figures, the reform has not raised costs.
entries.usage_note: Formal. In speech, "as far as I can tell" is far more common. Not "as far as one can say".

entries.headword: it remains to be seen whether
entries.definition: used to say that something is not yet known and will only become clear later
entries.example_academic: It remains to be seen whether the effect persists beyond the first year.
entries.example_spoken: It remains to be seen whether the new schedule actually works.
entries.example_interview: It remains to be seen whether I'll get the internship, but I'm hopeful.
entries.example_discussion: It remains to be seen whether the new rules will change behavior or simply move the problem elsewhere.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Useful to end a balanced argument. Followed by "whether" or a question word, not "if that".

entries.definition: mostly, in most cases or in most ways
entries.example_academic: For the most part, participants followed the instructions accurately.
entries.example_spoken: For the most part, the professors here are pretty approachable.
entries.example_interview: For the most part, my classmates were really welcoming when I arrived.
entries.example_discussion: For the most part, the evidence supports Daniel, although there are exceptions in rural areas.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Not "for the major part" or "for the most of part", two common French-influenced errors.

entries.definition: mostly, though not entirely
entries.example_academic: Urban growth was driven to a large extent by migration from rural areas.
entries.example_spoken: My grade depends to a large extent on the final project.
entries.example_interview: My choice of university was shaped to a large extent by my older sister.
entries.example_discussion: To a large extent, urban pollution is a transport problem rather than an industrial one.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Not "in a large extent". Stronger than "to some extent", weaker than "entirely".

entries.definition: used to show that a word or phrase is not meant literally
entries.example_academic: The new instruments opened a window, so to speak, onto the early universe.
entries.example_spoken: I'm the class's unofficial secretary, so to speak.
entries.example_interview: I was the group's translator, so to speak, because I was the only one who spoke Spanish.
entries.example_discussion: Social media acts as a mirror, so to speak, reflecting what users already believe.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Signals a figurative expression. Put it right after the image, not at the start of the sentence.

entries.definition: used to say that a statement is true when looked at in one particular way
entries.example_academic: In a sense, every map is an argument about what matters.
entries.example_spoken: In a sense, failing that test was the best thing that happened to me.
entries.example_interview: In a sense, moving abroad was my real education; I learned more outside class than in it.
entries.example_discussion: In a sense, both students are right, because they are talking about different time scales.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means "from one point of view". Not "in a way of speaking". Different from "in the sense that…".

entries.headword: it is fair to say that
entries.definition: used to make a claim that most people would accept as reasonable, often with some caution
entries.translation_fr: on peut dire que, il est juste de dire que
entries.example_academic: It is fair to say that the method has not yet been widely adopted.
entries.example_spoken: It is fair to say that I underestimated this course.
synonyms: it seems reasonable to say that
entries.example_interview: It is fair to say that my first semester was a steep learning curve.
entries.example_discussion: It is fair to say that the program has not reached the students who needed it most.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces a reasonable judgment. Do not write "it is right to say" in this sense.

entries.definition: used to say that something is reasonable to believe, though not proven
entries.example_academic: It seems plausible that the decline in bees is linked to several factors at once.
entries.example_spoken: It seems plausible that he just forgot about the meeting.
entries.example_interview: It seems plausible that I'll stay in this city after graduating, given my job prospects.
entries.example_discussion: It seems plausible that cheaper fares would attract new passengers, but we need evidence.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Plausible" = reasonable to believe, not "possible" in the sense of feasible.

entries.headword: there is reason to believe that
entries.definition: used to say that some evidence supports a belief, without claiming certainty
entries.example_academic: There is reason to believe that the manuscript was copied in two stages.
entries.example_spoken: There is reason to believe that the café will close next month.
entries.example_interview: There is reason to believe that our team will win this year; we've trained much harder.
entries.example_discussion: There is reason to believe that the decline will continue unless prices fall.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Not "there are reasons to think that" in academic writing, although that is understood.

entries.definition: used to report something that people say is true but that has not been proved
entries.example_academic: The documents were allegedly removed from the archive in the 1950s.
entries.example_spoken: He allegedly ate twelve slices of pizza in one sitting.
entries.example_interview: My cousin allegedly met the president once, but nobody in the family believes him.
entries.example_discussion: The company allegedly ignored early warnings, which would explain the scale of the problem.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Used to report a claim without endorsing it. Pronounced /əˈlɛdʒɪdli/, four syllables.

entries.definition: according to what people say or what has been reported
entries.translation_fr: à ce qu'on dit, selon les informations
entries.example_academic: The company is reportedly planning to close two of its research sites.
entries.example_spoken: The new gym is reportedly opening in March.
entries.example_interview: My favorite café is reportedly closing next month, which is a shame.
entries.example_discussion: The city is reportedly planning to close two libraries, which would affect Mia's argument.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, typical of news. Places responsibility for the information on the source.

entries.definition: after considering all the facts and arguments on both sides
entries.example_academic: On balance, the evidence favors a gradual rather than a sudden change.
entries.example_spoken: On balance, I'd rather live closer to campus and pay more.
entries.example_interview: On balance, I'd say studying abroad was worth the cost.
entries.example_discussion: On balance, I side with Kim, because the long-term savings outweigh the initial cost.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Excellent to announce a final position in Academic Discussion. Not "in balance".

entries.definition: in a general way, without considering the details or exceptions
entries.example_academic: Broadly speaking, the northern sites are older than the southern ones.
entries.example_spoken: Broadly speaking, I enjoyed the semester.
entries.example_interview: Broadly speaking, I'm a morning person, though exams change that.
entries.example_discussion: Broadly speaking, the two proposals pursue the same goal by different means.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Signals a generalization. Equivalent of "grosso modo"; "largely speaking" does not exist.

entries.definition: partly, but not completely
entries.example_academic: The theory works up to a point, but it cannot explain the later data.
entries.example_spoken: I agree with you up to a point.
entries.example_interview: I agree with you up to a point, but I'd never give up my car completely.
entries.example_discussion: Lena is right up to a point: incentives work, but only when the alternative is convenient.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Polite partial agreement. Not "until a certain point" in this sense.

entries.definition: used to say that something is true according to what you know, which may be incomplete
entries.example_academic: To my knowledge, no study has tested this effect in adults.
entries.example_spoken: To my knowledge, the deadline hasn't changed.
synonyms: to the best of my knowledge
entries.example_interview: To my knowledge, nobody in my family has ever studied abroad before me.
entries.example_discussion: To my knowledge, no study has compared the two methods in secondary schools.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Not "for my knowledge". "To the best of my knowledge" is even more formal.

entries.definition: used to propose an idea politely and with caution
entries.translation_fr: je me permettrais de suggérer que
entries.example_academic: I would tentatively suggest that the two effects share a common cause.
entries.example_spoken: I would tentatively suggest that we start a bit earlier next time.
entries.example_interview: I would tentatively suggest that we meet earlier next time; mornings seem easier for everyone.
entries.example_discussion: I would tentatively suggest that both solutions could be tested on a small scale first.
entries.usage_note: Formal and very polite. Useful when you disagree with the professor's framing without sounding blunt.

entries.definition: while having some doubts about something
entries.example_academic: The panel endorsed the proposal, with some reservations about its cost.
entries.example_spoken: I'd recommend the course, with some reservations.
entries.example_interview: I accepted the offer, with some reservations about the long commute.
entries.example_discussion: I support Lena's idea, with some reservations about who would run it.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Reservations" = doubts. It has nothing to do with booking a table here, a common confusion.

entries.definition: used to say politely that you believe something is true but could be wrong
entries.translation_fr: si je ne me trompe pas
entries.example_academic: If I'm not mistaken, the original study used a much smaller sample.
entries.example_spoken: If I'm not mistaken, the seminar's been moved to Thursday.
entries.example_interview: If I'm not mistaken, the museum is free on the first Sunday of the month.
entries.example_discussion: If I'm not mistaken, Jonah's figures come from a survey conducted before the pandemic.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, polite. Not "if I don't mistake". Use it to correct someone gently.

entries.definition: used before stating something you believe but are not completely sure about
entries.example_academic: Correct me if I'm wrong, but the second model assumes constant prices.
entries.example_spoken: Correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't we already pay for this?
entries.example_interview: Correct me if I'm wrong, but I think the deadline was extended.
entries.example_discussion: Correct me if I'm wrong, but the study Ana cites only included adults.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral, mostly spoken. Introduces a gentle correction or doubt, often followed by "but".

entries.definition: used to offer a guess when you are not sure of the answer
entries.example_academic: I'd hazard a guess that the inscription dates from the late Roman period.
entries.example_spoken: I'd hazard a guess that half the class hasn't started the essay.
entries.example_interview: I'd hazard a guess that most students here sleep less than seven hours.
entries.example_discussion: I'd hazard a guess that the effect would be smaller in rural schools.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Signals an educated guess. False friend: here "hazard" means "risk, venture", not French "hasard" (chance).

entries.definition: in most cases, but not always
entries.example_academic: More often than not, the first explanation offered turns out to be incomplete.
entries.example_spoken: More often than not, the bus is late on Mondays.
entries.example_interview: More often than not, I study better in the library than at home.
entries.example_discussion: More often than not, the cheapest option turns out to be the most expensive in the long run.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means "usually". Not "more often that not".

entries.definition: used to say that something is possible, even if not likely
entries.example_academic: The policy could conceivably increase inequality in the short term.
entries.example_spoken: We could conceivably finish tonight if nobody gets distracted.
entries.example_interview: I could conceivably finish my degree a semester early if I take summer classes.
entries.example_discussion: The tax could conceivably reduce consumption, but it would hit poorer households hardest.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Usually with "could" or "might". It suggests possibility, not likelihood.

entries.definition: judging by what can be seen, although the reality may differ
entries.example_academic: To all appearances, the two groups were equally motivated at the start.
entries.example_spoken: To all appearances, they're getting along fine.
entries.example_interview: To all appearances, my new roommate is very organized, but it's only been a week.
entries.example_discussion: To all appearances, the program is a success, yet no one has measured its effects.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Suggests that appearances might be misleading. "From all appearances" is also heard in American English.

entries.definition: used to accept that something is true, especially when it weakens your own argument
entries.example_academic: Admittedly, the sample was small, but the pattern was consistent across sites.
entries.example_spoken: Admittedly, I should have started the project sooner.
entries.example_interview: Admittedly, I wasn't the most organized student in my first year.
entries.example_discussion: Admittedly, the program is expensive, but Daniel ignores what inaction would cost.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Concedes a weakness in your own position. Often followed by "but". Very useful in Academic Discussion.

entries.definition: used to accept that something is true before making a point that goes against it
entries.example_academic: Granted, the method is expensive, yet no cheaper one gives reliable results.
entries.example_spoken: Granted, the room is small, but the location is perfect.
entries.example_interview: Granted, I'm not the fastest runner on the team, but I never miss training.
entries.example_discussion: Granted, online courses are cheaper; still, they rarely build a sense of community.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Concedes a point before countering it. Usually at the start of the sentence, followed by a comma.

entries.definition: used to accept a point before introducing a contrasting or more important one
entries.example_academic: While it is true that costs have risen, productivity has risen faster.
entries.example_spoken: While it is true that the course is hard, the teaching is excellent.
entries.example_interview: While it is true that I love cities, I could see myself living in the countryside one day.
entries.example_discussion: While it is true that cars pollute, banning them overnight would hurt rural workers.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Not "if it is true that", which expresses doubt rather than concession.

entries.headword: this is not to say that
entries.definition: used to prevent a reader from drawing a wrong or exaggerated conclusion from what was just said
entries.translation_fr: cela ne veut pas dire que
entries.example_academic: This is not to say that the earlier studies were worthless.
entries.example_spoken: This is not to say that I didn't enjoy the trip.
entries.example_interview: I enjoy studying alone; this is not to say that I don't like group projects.
entries.example_discussion: This is not to say that technology has no place in class, only that it should not replace teachers.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Prevents a misunderstanding. French speakers sometimes write "this does not want to say", a calque of "cela ne veut pas dire".

entries.definition: despite what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The data are incomplete. Even so, they point clearly in one direction.
entries.example_spoken: The tickets were expensive. Even so, we had a great time.
entries.example_interview: The tickets were expensive. Even so, it was the best concert I've ever been to.
entries.example_discussion: Lena's data are limited. Even so, they raise a question the professor should take seriously.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means "despite that". Do not confuse with "even if", which introduces a hypothesis.

entries.definition: despite what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The risk is small; all the same, it should be reported to participants.
entries.example_spoken: I know it's optional, but I'll go all the same.
entries.example_interview: I knew the hike would be hard, but I went all the same.
entries.example_discussion: The new rule may seem harsh; all the same, I think Mia is right to defend it.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often at the end of the clause in speech. Same as "nevertheless".

entries.definition: used to add something that contrasts with or limits what was just said
entries.example_academic: The results are encouraging. Having said that, the trial lasted only six weeks.
entries.example_spoken: The food was great. Having said that, the service was really slow.
entries.example_interview: The job pays well. Having said that, the hours are pretty long.
entries.example_discussion: The plan is well designed. Having said that, it ignores the cost of maintenance.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Very common in speech and discussion posts. Not "that being said that".

entries.definition: despite the thing that is mentioned
entries.example_academic: For all its ambition, the project produced few lasting results.
entries.example_spoken: For all his talk, he never actually turned up.
entries.example_interview: For all its noise, I really love living near the station.
entries.example_discussion: For all its benefits, the policy has not reached the students who need it most.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "For all + noun phrase" = despite. Not to be confused with "for all of us" (pour nous tous).

entries.definition: although; used to admit a feeling or a fact before saying something that contrasts with it
entries.example_academic: Much as the theory appeals to intuition, it lacks experimental support.
entries.example_spoken: Much as I love this city, I can't afford to stay.
entries.example_interview: Much as I love my hometown, I don't think I'll move back.
entries.example_discussion: Much as I sympathize with Lena's view, the numbers do not support it.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Much as I like X, …" = although I like X. Often with verbs of feeling.

entries.definition: whether it is; used to say that something is true in every case mentioned
entries.example_academic: Any change, be it economic or social, creates winners and losers.
entries.example_spoken: Any drink, be it coffee or tea, keeps me awake.
entries.example_interview: Any sport, be it running or swimming, helps me clear my head.
entries.example_discussion: Every student, be it in the city or the countryside, should have reliable internet.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Subjunctive structure: "be it X or Y" = whether it is X or Y. Similar to French "que ce soit".

entries.definition: without being affected or influenced by something
entries.example_academic: Participants received the same instructions regardless of their prior experience.
entries.example_spoken: I'm going regardless of the weather.
entries.example_interview: I try to sleep eight hours regardless of how much work I have.
entries.example_discussion: Students should have access to tutoring regardless of their income.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Not "regardless" alone before a noun, and never "irregardless" in careful English.

entries.definition: without considering or being influenced by something
entries.translation_fr: indépendamment de, sans tenir compte de
entries.example_academic: The law applies irrespective of the size of the company.
entries.example_spoken: You get the discount irrespective of your year of study.
entries.example_interview: My parents supported my choices irrespective of what they thought privately.
entries.example_discussion: Support should be available irrespective of whether students live on campus.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Same meaning as "regardless of"; slightly more formal, good in written answers.

entries.definition: used to accept, sometimes reluctantly, a point that weakens your position
entries.example_academic: It must be conceded that the archive covers only urban households.
entries.example_spoken: It must be conceded that my first draft was pretty weak.
synonyms: it has to be admitted that
entries.example_interview: It must be conceded that I wasn't very good at budgeting when I first moved out.
entries.example_discussion: It must be conceded that the critics have a point about the cost.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Strong written concession. The verb "concede" is transparent for French speakers; the passive structure is what matters.

entries.definition: used in speech to add something that limits or contrasts with what you have just said
entries.example_academic: The flat is tiny. Mind you, the rent is very low for this area.
entries.example_spoken: It was a hard exam. Mind you, I didn't study much.
entries.example_interview: My first job paid very little. Mind you, I learned more there than anywhere else.
entries.example_discussion: The plan is costly. Mind you, the alternative would cost even more in the long run.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Adds a qualification. Rare in formal writing; fine in an Interview answer.

entries.definition: used before saying something that makes a criticism less harsh or more balanced
entries.translation_fr: pour être juste, il faut dire que
entries.example_academic: To be fair, the authors acknowledge the limits of their sample.
entries.example_spoken: To be fair, he did warn us the class would be tough.
entries.example_interview: To be fair, my roommate did warn me about the noise.
entries.example_discussion: To be fair, Daniel does acknowledge the cost; he simply thinks it is worth paying.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Balances a criticism. "In fairness" is a slightly more formal variant.

entries.definition: used to introduce a point that contrasts with or limits what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The design is elegant. That being said, it has not been tested at scale.
entries.example_spoken: The internship doesn't pay much. That being said, it's great experience.
entries.example_interview: I loved the city. That being said, I wouldn't want to live there in winter.
entries.example_discussion: The proposal is ambitious. That being said, it lacks any clear funding plan.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Equivalent to "having said that". Avoid stacking several such markers in one post.

entries.definition: used to say that you are not judging something as a whole before criticizing one aspect of it
entries.translation_fr: quels que soient les mérites de
entries.example_academic: Whatever the merits of the proposal, it cannot be implemented this year.
entries.example_spoken: Whatever the merits of the plan, nobody wants to pay for it.
entries.example_interview: Whatever the merits of online shopping, I still prefer to see things before I buy them.
entries.example_discussion: Whatever the merits of Daniel's plan, it does not address the cost to families.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Sets aside a debate to focus on another point. Followed by a noun phrase.

entries.definition: used to accept a point while continuing to argue a different or stronger one
entries.example_academic: While acknowledging that the data are limited, the authors defend their main conclusion.
entries.example_spoken: While acknowledging that I was late, I'd like a second chance.
entries.example_interview: While acknowledging that I made mistakes, I'm proud of how the project turned out.
entries.example_discussion: While acknowledging that Kim's idea is cheap, I doubt it would reach the students who need it.
entries.usage_note: Formal. The verb is "acknowledge", with -dge; French speakers often misspell it "aknowledge".

entries.definition: used to contrast two actions, saying that the first is easier or different from the second
entries.translation_fr: une chose est de ..., une autre est de ...
entries.example_academic: It is one thing to identify a correlation and quite another to explain it.
entries.example_spoken: It is one thing to plan a trip and another thing to pay for it.
synonyms: it is easy to... but harder to
entries.example_interview: It is one thing to set a goal and another thing to stick to it, as I learned last year.
entries.example_discussion: It is one thing to ban phones in class and quite another to enforce the ban.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Two-part structure: "It is one thing to X and (quite) another to Y". Do not drop the second part.

entries.definition: however; used in speech, often at the end of a sentence, to add a contrasting point
entries.example_academic: The method is slow. It is far more reliable, though.
entries.example_spoken: The movie was long. I liked it, though.
entries.example_interview: My hometown is small. I'd love to go back one day, though.
entries.example_discussion: The policy is expensive. It would pay for itself within a decade, though.
entries.usage_note: Informal at the end of a sentence. Different from "although", which starts a clause. Very natural in Interview answers.

entries.definition: used to introduce a fact that should also be considered and that contrasts with what was just said
entries.example_academic: The reform cut waiting times; at the same time, it reduced the number of specialists.
entries.example_spoken: I want to travel. At the same time, I need to save money.
entries.example_interview: I love my job. At the same time, I know I'll need a degree to progress.
entries.example_discussion: Technology helps students; at the same time, it can be a constant distraction.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Here it introduces a contrasting consideration, not simultaneity. Context makes the sense clear.

entries.definition: used to introduce a surprising contrast with what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The theory was elegant and widely accepted, and yet it was wrong.
entries.example_spoken: I studied for days, and yet I blanked on the first question.
entries.example_interview: I was terrified of public speaking, and yet I volunteered to give the welcome talk.
entries.example_discussion: The city spends more than ever on transport, and yet congestion keeps rising.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Stresses a surprising contrast. More emphatic than "but".

entries.definition: despite that additional condition or effort
entries.translation_fr: même alors, même dans ce cas
entries.example_academic: Even then, only a third of the participants completed the course.
entries.example_spoken: I reread the instructions twice, and even then I got it wrong.
entries.example_interview: I practiced my speech every night, and even then my hands were shaking on the day.
entries.example_discussion: Even then, as Mia notes, only a minority of students used the new service.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Even in that case". Different from "even so" (despite that).

entries.definition: used to add a fact or thought that contrasts with what you just said
entries.translation_fr: d'un autre côté, mais en même temps
entries.example_academic: The drug works quickly. Then again, its effects do not last long.
entries.example_spoken: The bigger room is nicer. Then again, it's much more expensive.
entries.example_interview: I'd love a bigger room. Then again, I'm hardly ever there.
entries.example_discussion: Online courses are cheaper. Then again, completion rates are much lower.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Adds a counter-consideration, often in speech. Not "and again".

entries.definition: on the condition that something specific is true or is done
entries.translation_fr: à condition que, sous réserve que
entries.example_academic: The committee approved the study with the proviso that consent forms be revised.
entries.example_spoken: I'll lend you my notes, with the proviso that you return them by Friday.
entries.example_interview: My parents agreed to lend me the car, with the proviso that I pay for the fuel.
entries.example_discussion: I would accept the plan, with the proviso that it is reviewed after one year.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "on condition that". Pronounced /prəˈvaɪzoʊ/.

entries.definition: used to give at least one reason for something, even if there are no others
entries.example_academic: The study deserves attention, if only because it challenges a common assumption.
entries.example_spoken: You should go, if only because the food is free.
synonyms: if for no other reason than
entries.example_interview: I'm glad I took that class, if only because I met my best friend there.
entries.example_discussion: The program deserves funding, if only because nothing else is available in rural areas.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Gives at least one reason. Not "only if because", a frequent scrambling.

entries.definition: used to draw attention to the most surprising or noticeable fact
entries.example_academic: What is striking is how quickly the new technique spread across the region.
entries.example_spoken: What is striking is how calm everyone stayed.
entries.example_interview: What is striking is how quickly I got used to the new routine.
entries.example_discussion: What is striking is that both students agree on the goal but not on the means.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. A pseudo-cleft that puts the key observation first. In speech, "what's striking is" is also fine.

entries.definition: used to emphasize one important example or reason among several
entries.example_academic: The project faced many obstacles, not least the lack of reliable funding.
entries.example_spoken: It was a great trip, not least because of the people we met.
entries.example_interview: I chose this university for many reasons, not least its music program.
entries.example_discussion: Lena's proposal has many advantages, not least its low cost.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "especially". Not "not the least" in this use.

entries.definition: more than anything else; used to stress what is most important
entries.example_academic: The archive is, first and foremost, a record of ordinary working lives.
entries.example_spoken: First and foremost, I'm here to learn.
entries.example_interview: First and foremost, I'm a student; my job comes second.
entries.example_discussion: First and foremost, any reform should protect the students who need help most.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Stresses priority. Do not use it for a simple list order ("firstly").

entries.definition: not at all; used to emphasize a negative statement
entries.example_academic: The results are by no means conclusive.
entries.example_spoken: It's by no means the worst dorm on campus.
entries.example_interview: It was by no means an easy decision to change majors.
entries.example_discussion: The evidence is by no means conclusive, as Mia herself admits.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Strong negative. Not "by no way". Different from "by all means" (please do).

entries.definition: not at all, in any respect
entries.example_academic: The findings in no way justify cutting the program.
entries.example_spoken: That in no way excuses being rude to the staff.
entries.example_interview: That in no way changed my mind about the course.
entries.example_discussion: A single bad result in no way proves that the method is useless.
entries.usage_note: Formal. At the start of a sentence, it requires inversion: "In no way does this justify…".

entries.definition: used to say that something is not true at all, or is the opposite of what is expected
entries.example_academic: Far from reducing traffic, the new road attracted more cars.
entries.example_spoken: Far from being boring, the lecture was the best of the term.
entries.example_interview: Far from discouraging me, failing my first exam made me work twice as hard.
entries.example_discussion: Far from saving money, the policy Kim defends would shift costs to families.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Far from + -ing" = the opposite is true. French speakers sometimes write "far of", a calque of "loin de".

entries.definition: used to say that something has at least one good result, even if it has no others
entries.translation_fr: à défaut d'autre chose, au moins
entries.example_academic: If nothing else, the controversy drew attention to a neglected problem.
entries.example_spoken: If nothing else, the trip taught me how to pack light.
entries.example_interview: If nothing else, my year abroad taught me to be patient.
entries.example_discussion: If nothing else, Daniel's post shows how little data we have on this question.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "At least". Placed at the start of the sentence.

entries.definition: even more than before or than expected, for the reason given
entries.example_academic: The discovery is all the more remarkable given the poor condition of the site.
entries.example_spoken: That makes the win all the more satisfying.
entries.example_interview: Winning was all the more satisfying because nobody expected it.
entries.example_discussion: The result is all the more surprising given the small sample.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "All the more + adjective + because/given…". Equivalent to "d'autant plus".

entries.definition: used after a negative statement to say that something else is even less likely
entries.example_academic: Few households could afford a radio, let alone a television.
entries.example_spoken: I can barely cook pasta, let alone a three-course meal.
entries.example_interview: When I arrived, I couldn't order a coffee in English, let alone give a presentation.
entries.example_discussion: Many schools cannot afford textbooks, let alone tablets for every student.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Used after a negative. French speakers often put it after a positive sentence, which sounds wrong.

entries.definition: used to add a further point that makes the situation even more extreme
entries.example_academic: The project cost millions, to say nothing of the damage to the company's reputation.
entries.example_spoken: The rent is high, to say nothing of the bills.
entries.example_interview: Moving cities was expensive, to say nothing of the stress.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's plan would cost millions, to say nothing of the time needed to train staff.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Adds a further, stronger point. Same function as "not to mention".

entries.definition: used to stress that the reason given is exactly the cause, often a surprising one
entries.example_academic: The theory was accepted precisely because it was so simple.
entries.example_spoken: I liked the course precisely because it was difficult.
entries.example_interview: I chose this program precisely because it includes an internship.
entries.example_discussion: The policy works precisely because it is simple to understand.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Stresses that the reason is exactly this one, often a surprising one.

entries.definition: used to say that something is extremely important
entries.translation_fr: on ne saurait trop insister sur
entries.example_academic: It cannot be overstated how much the archive owes to its volunteer transcribers.
entries.example_spoken: Honestly, it cannot be overstated how helpful the tutors were.
entries.example_interview: It cannot be overstated how much my teachers shaped my choices.
entries.example_discussion: It cannot be overstated how much rural students depend on public transport.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "it is extremely important". French speakers sometimes misread it as "it should not be exaggerated".

entries.definition: used to draw the reader's attention to a point that is especially important
entries.example_academic: It is worth stressing that the effect appeared in every age group.
entries.example_spoken: It is worth stressing that late submissions get zero.
entries.example_interview: It is worth stressing that I did all of this while working part time.
entries.example_discussion: It is worth stressing that Mia's figures come from a single school.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Draws attention to a key point. "It is worth + -ing", never "it is worth to stress".

entries.headword: nowhere is this more evident than
entries.definition: used to introduce the clearest example of something just described
entries.translation_fr: cela n'est nulle part plus manifeste que
entries.example_academic: Nowhere is this more evident than in the housing market of large cities.
entries.example_spoken: Nowhere is this more evident than in the dining hall at lunchtime.
entries.example_interview: Nowhere is this more evident than in my family, where everyone speaks three languages.
entries.example_discussion: Nowhere is this more evident than in the long queues Lena describes at the start of term.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Requires inversion after "nowhere". A strong way to introduce your best example.

entries.definition: used to stress that something happened only after a particular time or event
entries.translation_fr: ce n'est qu'en ... que, il a fallu attendre ... pour que
entries.example_academic: It was not until the 1960s that the theory gained wide acceptance.
entries.example_spoken: It was not until I moved here that I learned to cook.
entries.example_interview: It was not until my second year that I really enjoyed my studies.
entries.example_discussion: It was not until the 1990s that the problem received serious attention.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "It was not until X that Y" = Y only happened after X. French speakers often drop the "that".

entries.definition: much more than what is required or expected
entries.example_academic: The volunteers worked above and beyond what their contracts required.
entries.example_spoken: Our tutor went above and beyond to help us before the exam.
entries.example_interview: My manager went above and beyond to help me settle in.
entries.example_discussion: Teachers who go above and beyond deserve recognition, but not in the form of unpaid hours.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Go above and beyond" = do much more than required.

entries.definition: because of its own qualities, not because of its connection with something else
entries.example_academic: The documentary is a work of art in its own right.
entries.example_spoken: The bakery is worth a visit in its own right.
entries.example_interview: Cooking has become a hobby in its own right for me, not just a necessity.
entries.example_discussion: Music should be valued as a subject in its own right, not as a break from math.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Means "independently, on its own merits". "In his/her own right" for people.

entries.definition: used to say something very directly, even if it may sound harsh
entries.example_academic: To put it bluntly, the current model cannot explain the new observations.
entries.example_spoken: To put it bluntly, your essay doesn't answer the question.
entries.example_interview: To put it bluntly, my first apartment was a disaster.
entries.example_discussion: To put it bluntly, the current plan cannot work without more staff.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, direct. Signals frankness. Use sparingly in written answers.

entries.definition: used to emphasize that what you are saying is completely true
entries.example_academic: Make no mistake, these changes will affect every department.
entries.example_spoken: Make no mistake, this exam counts for half your grade.
entries.example_interview: Make no mistake, I know this role is demanding, and that's why I want it.
entries.example_discussion: Make no mistake: without funding, Kim's plan will stay on paper.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, emphatic. Typical of speeches. Not "do no mistake".

entries.definition: used to add that the true situation may be the opposite of what was suggested, or even stronger
entries.translation_fr: au contraire, si tant est que
entries.example_academic: The new policy has not reduced inequality; if anything, it has increased it.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not tired. If anything, I'm full of energy.
entries.example_interview: Living alone didn't make me lonely; if anything, it made me more sociable.
entries.example_discussion: Shorter holidays would not help students; if anything, they would increase burnout.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Suggests the truth may be the opposite of what was said. Not "if something".

entries.definition: used to introduce the most important point
entries.example_academic: Crucially, the effect disappeared when participants were told the purpose of the test.
entries.example_spoken: Crucially, you need to register before Friday.
entries.example_interview: Crucially, I had a mentor who believed in me.
entries.example_discussion: Crucially, none of the studies Jonah cites followed students for more than a year.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces the most important point. Overused in some essays; one per answer is enough.

entries.definition: used to stress a point by saying it again
entries.translation_fr: il n'est pas inutile de rappeler que
entries.example_academic: It bears repeating that correlation alone does not establish cause.
entries.example_spoken: It bears repeating that the library closes early on Fridays.
entries.example_interview: It bears repeating that I had no training before that first job.
entries.example_discussion: It bears repeating that Mia's survey only included volunteers.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "it is worth saying again". "Bears" here means "deserves", not the animal.

entries.definition: used to add a further and more important point
entries.example_academic: The method is cheaper; what is more, it gives faster results.
entries.example_spoken: The flat is close to campus. What is more, it has a garden.
entries.example_interview: I speak three languages. What is more, I've worked in international teams.
entries.example_discussion: Free transport would reduce traffic; what is more, it would help low-income students most.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Adds a stronger point. "What's more" in speech. Not "what more is".

entries.definition: used to introduce something that is more important or relevant than what was just said
entries.example_academic: The plan is expensive and, more to the point, it has never been tested.
entries.example_spoken: The café is far. More to the point, it closes at six.
entries.example_interview: I could live with my parents. More to the point, I want to be independent.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel's plan is costly and, more to the point, nobody has asked students what they want.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces something more relevant than what was just said.

entries.definition: used before an adjective or adverb to stress that something unwelcome is very true
entries.example_academic: Such accidents are all too common in older factories.
entries.example_spoken: I know that feeling all too well.
entries.example_interview: I know all too well how hard it is to study while working.
entries.example_discussion: Students are all too often left out of decisions that affect them, as Kim says.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "All too + adjective/adverb" stresses that something unwelcome is very true.

entries.definition: used in speech to introduce the main problem or explanation
entries.example_academic: The thing is, the original data were never published.
entries.example_spoken: The thing is, I've already promised to help someone else.
entries.example_interview: The thing is, I've never really liked studying in silence.
entries.example_discussion: The thing is, nobody has asked the teachers what they need.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Introduces the real issue. In writing, "the problem is" or "the key point is".

entries.definition: used to introduce the most important idea in what you are saying
entries.example_academic: The point is, no single measure can capture the whole picture.
entries.example_spoken: The point is, we need to start earlier.
entries.example_interview: The point is, I learned more from that failure than from any success.
entries.example_discussion: The point is that the policy helps those who need it least.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Brings the conversation back to the essential idea.

entries.definition: used to introduce your personal view of a situation
entries.example_academic: The way I see it, the policy shifts the burden onto local governments.
entries.example_spoken: The way I see it, we have two options.
entries.example_interview: The way I see it, university is about learning to think, not just getting a job.
entries.example_discussion: The way I see it, both proposals could work if they were combined.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Introduces a personal view. A good alternative to "in my opinion".

entries.definition: used in speech to give your opinion, often one that others may not share
entries.example_academic: If you ask me, the study raises more questions than it answers.
entries.example_spoken: If you ask me, the old schedule was better.
entries.example_interview: If you ask me, the best part of the city is the riverside.
entries.example_discussion: If you ask me, the professor's question assumes a false choice.
entries.usage_note: Informal. A personal opinion, sometimes slightly provocative.

entries.definition: used when you suddenly remember or realize something while speaking
entries.example_academic: Come to think of it, the same pattern appears in the earlier survey.
entries.example_spoken: Come to think of it, I haven't seen him all week.
synonyms: now that I think about it
entries.example_interview: Come to think of it, my interest in languages probably started with travel.
entries.example_discussion: Come to think of it, Sara's example comes from the same region as the study.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Signals a thought that has just occurred to you.

entries.definition: used to return to what you were talking about before an interruption
entries.example_academic: As I was saying, the second phase of the project begins in May.
entries.example_spoken: Anyway, as I was saying, the party starts at eight.
synonyms: to get back to the point
entries.example_interview: Anyway, as I was saying, that summer changed my plans completely.
