entries.example_discussion: As I was saying in my earlier post, funding is the real obstacle.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Returns to a point after an interruption or digression.

entries.headword: to cut a long story short
entries.definition: used to skip the details and give only the main point
entries.example_academic: To cut a long story short, the funding was approved after three rounds of review.
entries.example_spoken: To cut a long story short, I missed the train.
entries.example_interview: To cut a long story short, I ended up studying the subject I liked least at school.
entries.example_discussion: To cut a long story short, the pilot project failed because nobody used it.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Skips details to reach the outcome. Not "to make a long story short" in British English, though American English uses that.

entries.headword: at the end of the day
entries.definition: used to give what you think is the most important fact after considering everything
entries.example_academic: At the end of the day, the decision depends on how much risk society accepts.
entries.example_spoken: At the end of the day, it's your choice.
synonyms: when all is said and done
entries.example_interview: At the end of the day, I chose the university that felt right.
entries.example_discussion: At the end of the day, the decision depends on what we value more: cost or quality.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Means "ultimately". Overused by some speakers; avoid it more than once per answer.

entries.definition: used to introduce the particular subject you are talking about
entries.translation_fr: quand il s'agit de, en matière de
entries.example_academic: When it comes to long-term memory, sleep plays a central role.
entries.example_spoken: When it comes to cooking, I'm hopeless.
entries.example_interview: When it comes to teamwork, I'm usually the one who keeps track of deadlines.
entries.example_discussion: When it comes to public health, prevention is usually cheaper than treatment.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "When it comes to + noun or -ing". Not "when it comes to + infinitive".

entries.definition: used to mention a fact that is surprising or relevant by chance
entries.example_academic: As it happens, the same village appears in an earlier census.
entries.example_spoken: As it happens, I'm free that afternoon.
entries.example_interview: As it happens, I've already used the software you mentioned.
entries.example_discussion: As it happens, the city tried a similar scheme in 2015.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces a relevant coincidence or fact.

entries.headword: let me put it this way
entries.definition: used before explaining something in a different or clearer way
entries.example_academic: Let me put it this way: the model works only if prices stay stable.
entries.example_spoken: Let me put it this way, I won't be taking that class again.
entries.example_interview: Let me put it this way: I've never missed a deadline in three years.
entries.example_discussion: Let me put it this way: a policy nobody understands is a policy nobody will follow.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Rephrases more clearly or more tactfully. Followed by a colon in writing.

entries.definition: used to introduce the most basic and important fact in a situation
entries.example_academic: The bottom line is that the program costs more than it saves.
entries.example_spoken: The bottom line is, we need more volunteers.
entries.example_interview: The bottom line is, I need a job that fits around my classes.
entries.example_discussion: The bottom line is that no plan works if teachers are not consulted.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Introduces the essential fact. From accounting ("the last line of a budget").

entries.definition: used to move to a topic that is connected to the one just discussed
entries.example_academic: On a related note, similar effects have been reported in urban birds.
entries.example_spoken: On a related note, has anyone booked the room for Friday?
entries.example_interview: On a related note, I've also started learning Italian.
entries.example_discussion: On a related note, the same issue affects public libraries.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Moves to a connected topic without breaking the flow.

entries.definition: used in a talk to move to the next point
entries.example_academic: That brings me to the second limitation of the study: its sample size.
entries.example_spoken: That brings me to my last question.
entries.example_interview: That brings me to the main reason I applied for this program.
entries.example_discussion: That brings me to my second objection to Kim's proposal.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Signposts the next point in a talk or post.

entries.definition: used to return to a point mentioned earlier in a discussion
entries.example_academic: Going back to your earlier question, the data were collected in 2019.
entries.example_spoken: Going back to what Sam said, I think we should vote.
entries.example_interview: Going back to what you asked earlier, I started playing piano at six.
entries.example_discussion: Going back to the professor's question, I think the answer depends on age.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Returns to an earlier point. "Going back to + noun phrase".

entries.definition: used to say what the real situation was, often different from what was expected
entries.translation_fr: en fin de compte, il s'avère que
entries.example_academic: As it turns out, the effect was caused by a faulty instrument.
entries.example_spoken: As it turns out, the class was cancelled anyway.
entries.example_interview: As it turns out, the class I almost dropped became my favorite.
entries.example_discussion: As it turns out, the first study had a serious flaw.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Reveals the real situation, often a surprise.

entries.definition: used to introduce something that is obvious or expected
entries.example_academic: Needless to say, the results must be confirmed in a larger sample.
entries.example_spoken: Needless to say, I didn't get much sleep.
entries.example_interview: Needless to say, my first attempt at cooking for twelve people was chaotic.
entries.example_discussion: Needless to say, any reform needs the support of teachers.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces something obvious; use it for emphasis, not literally.

entries.definition: used to introduce the last item of a list while stressing that it is not the least important
entries.example_academic: Last but not least, the authors thank the families who took part.
entries.example_spoken: Last but not least, don't forget your ID.
entries.example_interview: Last but not least, I want to mention my sister, who encouraged me.
entries.example_discussion: Last but not least, the cost to taxpayers must be considered.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces the final item while stressing its importance.

entries.definition: used to explain more exactly what you have just said
entries.example_academic: The effect was transient, that is to say, it vanished within a week.
entries.example_spoken: We're meeting on the fifteenth, that is to say next Tuesday.
entries.example_interview: I'm a night owl, that is to say, I work best after ten.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's proposal is regressive, that is to say, it costs poorer families more.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Clarifies or restates. In speech, "I mean" or "in other words" is more natural.

entries.definition: used to introduce a brief summary of what has been said
entries.example_academic: In short, the evidence does not support the original claim.
entries.example_spoken: In short, it was a disaster.
entries.example_interview: In short, it was the best decision I've ever made.
entries.example_discussion: In short, Lena's plan is fair but too expensive to work.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces a brief summary. Not "in shortly".

entries.definition: in order to achieve the aim that has just been mentioned
entries.translation_fr: à cette fin, dans ce but
entries.example_academic: The city aims to halve emissions. To that end, it is expanding public transport.
entries.example_spoken: I want to improve my speaking. To that end, I joined a conversation club.
entries.example_interview: I want to work abroad. To that end, I'm taking an extra language course.
entries.example_discussion: The city wants fewer cars downtown. To that end, it has expanded bus routes.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "for that purpose". Different from "in the end" (finally).

entries.definition: as a result of something that happened before, in a chain of effects
entries.example_academic: Higher prices reduced demand, which in turn led to job losses.
entries.example_spoken: I helped her, and she in turn helped her roommate.
entries.example_interview: My teacher inspired me, and I in turn try to help younger students.
entries.example_discussion: Better sleep improves focus, which in turn raises grades, as Daniel argues.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Describes a chain of effects or a reciprocal action.

entries.definition: used to introduce the first of several reasons
entries.example_academic: The theory is hard to test. For one thing, the effects are extremely small.
entries.example_spoken: I can't go. For one thing, I have a lab report due.
entries.example_interview: I can't move there. For one thing, the rent is far too high.
entries.example_discussion: The plan is unrealistic. For one thing, it ignores maintenance costs.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Gives a first reason, implying there are others.

entries.definition: for the same reasons; used to show that a related point is also true
entries.translation_fr: de la même manière, par la même occasion
entries.example_academic: Strong institutions attract investment; by the same token, weak ones discourage it.
entries.example_spoken: If you can be late, then by the same token so can I.
entries.example_interview: If I expect honesty from my friends, then by the same token I have to be honest with them.
entries.example_discussion: If schools can ban phones, then by the same token they could ban laptops, which seems absurd.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Applies the same reasoning to a related case.

entries.definition: used to end a conversation or a part of it, often by moving to a related final point
entries.example_academic: On that note, I will turn to the questions from the audience.
entries.example_spoken: On that note, I'm going to get some sleep.
entries.example_interview: On that note, I think I've said everything about my hometown.
entries.example_discussion: On that note, I will leave the final word to Mia.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Closes a topic or moves to a final remark.

entries.definition: used before giving a simple explanation of something complicated
entries.translation_fr: pour faire simple, en termes simples
entries.example_academic: To put it simply, the vaccine teaches the body to recognize the virus.
entries.example_spoken: To put it simply, we ran out of money.
entries.example_interview: To put it simply, I love teaching.
entries.example_discussion: To put it simply, the tax shifts the cost from drivers to everyone.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Introduces a simplified explanation.

entries.definition: used to add a less important piece of information or to introduce a new topic
entries.translation_fr: au fait, soit dit en passant
entries.example_academic: Incidentally, the same author later revised several of these conclusions.
entries.example_spoken: Incidentally, have you seen my blue notebook?
entries.example_interview: Incidentally, that's also where I met my best friend.
entries.example_discussion: Incidentally, the study Mia cites was funded by a phone company.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Adds a side remark. Not "accidentally", which means by mistake.

entries.definition: in a very short and clear way
entries.example_academic: In a nutshell, the reform shifted power from the center to the regions.
entries.example_spoken: In a nutshell, the course is about how markets fail.
entries.example_interview: In a nutshell, I'm organized, curious and good with people.
entries.example_discussion: In a nutshell, Jonah's proposal is cheap but unfair.
entries.usage_note: Informal. A very short summary. Not suitable for formal essays, fine in speech.

entries.definition: used in speech to add a further problem or issue to be considered
entries.translation_fr: et puis il y a la question de
entries.example_academic: Then there's the question of who will pay for maintenance.
entries.example_spoken: Then there's the question of where we'd all sleep.
entries.example_interview: I'd love to study abroad; then there's the question of how I'd pay for it.
entries.example_discussion: Then there's the question of who decides which students qualify, which none of the posts address.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Adds another issue to consider.

entries.definition: used in a talk to introduce the final point or summary
entries.example_academic: To round off, I will summarize the three main findings.
entries.example_spoken: To round off, let's look at next week's schedule.
entries.example_interview: To round off, I'd say this experience made me more independent.
entries.example_discussion: To round off, the evidence suggests a cautious approach.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Signals the end of a talk or answer.

entries.definition: used to accept that what someone has said is valid, often before disagreeing in part
entries.translation_fr: je vois ce que vous voulez dire, j'entends bien
entries.example_academic: I take your point about cost, but the long-term savings are considerable.
entries.example_spoken: I take your point, but I still think we should wait.
entries.example_interview: I take your point about the cost, but I'd still choose the smaller college.
entries.example_discussion: I take your point, Marco, but the evidence you mention is from a very different context.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Accepts an argument before disagreeing. "I take your point, but…" is a polite opener in Academic Discussion.

entries.definition: used to say that you agree with an idea or a suggestion
entries.example_academic: I'd go along with that interpretation, provided the dates are confirmed.
entries.example_spoken: Pizza tonight? Yeah, I'd go along with that.
entries.example_interview: If my friends want to cook together on Sundays, I'd go along with that.
entries.example_discussion: I'd go along with that proposal, provided the schedule is flexible.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Means agree or accept. In writing, "I would support that" is more formal.

entries.definition: used to say politely that you are not sure something is true
entries.example_academic: You say the policy succeeded, but that's debatable given the later figures.
entries.example_spoken: He says it's the best café in town. That's debatable.
entries.example_interview: My brother says I'm the messy one at home, but that's debatable.
entries.example_discussion: Lena calls the policy a success; that's debatable, given the drop in attendance.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, slightly informal. A short way to disagree without being rude. In writing, "that is debatable".

entries.definition: used to express polite doubt about a claim
entries.translation_fr: je ne suis pas convaincu que
entries.example_academic: I'm not convinced that the sample represents the wider population.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not convinced that this is the quickest route.
entries.example_interview: I'm not convinced that working at night suits me, so I'm looking for a day job.
entries.example_discussion: I'm not convinced that higher fines would change drivers' behavior.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Polite disagreement. Followed by a clause, not by "of that".

entries.headword: I see where you're coming from
entries.definition: used to show that you understand someone's reasons, often before disagreeing
entries.translation_fr: je comprends votre point de vue
entries.example_academic: I see where you're coming from, but the data point the other way.
entries.example_spoken: I see where you're coming from, but I'd still rather stay in.
entries.example_interview: I see where you're coming from, but I think a gap year can be useful.
entries.example_discussion: I see where you're coming from, Sara, but the costs fall on taxpayers, not just users.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Shows understanding before disagreeing. Not "I see from where you come".

entries.definition: used to admit that what someone said is true or reasonable
entries.example_academic: You have a point there: the earlier figures did exclude rural areas.
entries.example_spoken: You have a point there, the bus is faster at night.
entries.example_interview: You have a point there; I hadn't thought about the cost of travel.
entries.example_discussion: You have a point there, Jonah: the policy does ignore part-time workers.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Concedes that someone is partly right. Not "you have a point here" in this sense.

entries.definition: used to express doubt about whether something is true or appropriate
entries.translation_fr: je me demande si, je doute que
entries.example_academic: I'd question whether the survey measured attitudes or simply habits.
entries.example_spoken: I'd question whether we really need three meetings a week.
entries.example_interview: When people say a degree guarantees a job, I'd question whether that's still true.
entries.example_discussion: I'd question whether a ban would change anything if parents keep buying phones for younger children.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Polite doubt. Followed by "whether", not "if that".

entries.headword: that's only part of the story
entries.definition: used to say that an explanation is true but incomplete
entries.translation_fr: ce n'est qu'une partie de l'explication
entries.example_academic: Prices did rise, but that's only part of the story; wages rose too.
entries.example_spoken: Sure, the professor was strict, but that's only part of the story.
entries.example_interview: Sure, the job pays well, but that's only part of the story; the hours are terrible.
entries.example_discussion: Higher wages matter, but that's only part of the story: housing costs have risen faster.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Points out that an explanation is incomplete.

entries.headword: I couldn't have put it better
entries.definition: used to say that you agree completely with how someone has expressed something
entries.example_academic: I couldn't have put it better myself: the problem is coordination, not money.
entries.example_spoken: I couldn't have put it better. That's exactly how I feel.
entries.example_interview: My friend said the trip was "tiring but worth every minute", and I couldn't have put it better.
entries.example_discussion: Mia says the rule punishes the wrong students, and I couldn't have put it better.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Strong agreement. Not "I couldn't have said better", which is incomplete.

entries.definition: used to accept that what someone said is reasonable, even if you do not fully agree
entries.example_academic: Fair enough, the second sample was larger, but it came from one city.
entries.example_spoken: You need a break? Fair enough.
entries.example_interview: Fair enough, I'll take the earlier train if it makes things easier.
entries.example_discussion: Fair enough, Kim, but cheaper is not always better for students.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Accepts a point as reasonable, sometimes reluctantly. Avoid it in formal written answers.

entries.definition: used to compare two things and show how different the second one is
entries.example_academic: Northern sites are well preserved; by contrast, the southern ones are badly eroded.
entries.example_spoken: My sister loves the city. By contrast, I'd rather live by the sea.
entries.example_interview: My high school was tiny; by contrast, my university has thirty thousand students.
entries.example_discussion: Public transport is cheap in Lena's city; by contrast, it is almost absent in rural areas.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Compares two different things. Not "at the contrary", a frequent French calque.

entries.definition: used to say that the opposite of what was just said is true
entries.example_academic: The reform did not reduce costs; on the contrary, it increased them.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not bored at all. On the contrary, I'm loving it.
entries.example_interview: Moving abroad didn't make me homesick; on the contrary, it made me more independent.
entries.example_discussion: The ban did not reduce smoking; on the contrary, the figures show a slight increase.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Contradicts a statement. French speakers overuse it for simple contrast, where "by contrast" or "on the other hand" is correct.

entries.headword: that is not to deny that
entries.definition: used to accept a point while making clear that your argument still stands
entries.translation_fr: je ne nie pas pour autant que
entries.example_academic: The policy has flaws; that is not to deny that it helped many families.
entries.example_spoken: It was stressful. That is not to deny that I learned a lot.
entries.example_interview: My first job was exhausting. That is not to deny that it taught me a great deal.
entries.example_discussion: Technology can distract students; that is not to deny that it also opens new ways of learning.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Prevents your criticism from sounding absolute. Close to "this is not to say that".

entries.definition: despite what has just been said
entries.example_academic: The method is slow and costly; for all that, it remains the most reliable.
entries.example_spoken: He's a bit rude. For all that, I like working with him.
entries.example_interview: The commute is long. For all that, I wouldn't change jobs.
entries.example_discussion: The study has a small sample; for all that, its conclusions match earlier research.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "nevertheless". Not "for all this" in the same sense, though it is understood.

entries.definition: used to make a contrast between two things
entries.example_academic: The study measured actual behavior, as opposed to what people said they did.
entries.example_spoken: I prefer working in the morning, as opposed to late at night.
entries.example_interview: I like learning by doing, as opposed to just listening to lectures.
entries.example_discussion: We should measure what students can do, as opposed to how many hours they sit in class.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Followed by a noun or -ing. Not "opposed to" alone in this sense.

entries.definition: in a way that is the opposite of what someone expected or claimed
entries.example_academic: Contrary to earlier claims, the drug had no effect on memory.
entries.example_spoken: Contrary to what I expected, the exam was quite easy.
entries.example_interview: Contrary to what my parents thought, I actually enjoyed boarding school.
entries.example_discussion: Contrary to Jonah's assumption, most students in the survey supported the new rule.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Contrary to popular belief / to what X said". French speakers often use it to compare two people ("contrary to my brother"), where "unlike" is correct.

entries.definition: used to show that something happened after an action and made the action useless or disappointing
entries.example_academic: Researchers spent years on the project, only to see it cancelled.
entries.example_spoken: I ran to the station, only to find the train had left.
entries.example_interview: I studied for weeks, only to find out the exam had been moved.
entries.example_discussion: Many towns build large stadiums only to see them empty after one event.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Structure: "…, only to + infinitive". Expresses a disappointing outcome, not purpose.

entries.definition: used to say that something seems true at first, although it may not be
entries.example_academic: On the face of it, the results support the theory, but the sample was very small.
entries.example_spoken: On the face of it, it's a great deal. Read the small print, though.
entries.example_interview: On the face of it, the job looked perfect, but the hours were impossible.
entries.example_discussion: On the face of it, Kim's plan is cheaper, yet it ignores the cost of maintenance.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Prepares a contrast with reality. Not "in the face of it", which means something else.

entries.definition: used to accept that an idea is partly correct before adding a reservation
entries.translation_fr: il y a du vrai dans
entries.example_academic: There is some truth in the claim, but it ignores regional differences.
entries.example_spoken: There is some truth in what you're saying.
entries.example_interview: There is some truth in the idea that you learn more from failure, but it isn't fun at the time.
entries.example_discussion: There is some truth in Daniel's argument, but he overlooks students who work part time.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Polite partial agreement. "There is some truth in/to it". Not "there is a truth in".

entries.definition: used to accept that something is possibly true, often before an objection
entries.example_academic: It may well be that the effect is real, but the study cannot prove it.
entries.example_spoken: It may well be that he's busy, but he could still reply.
entries.example_interview: It may well be that I'll change careers one day, but for now I love this field.
entries.example_discussion: It may well be that the policy reduces costs, but at what price for quality?
entries.usage_note: Formal. "May well" = it is quite possible. Often followed by "but". Not "it can well be that".

entries.definition: used in speech to introduce what you find most surprising or important
entries.example_academic: What strikes me is how little the debate has changed in twenty years.
entries.example_spoken: What strikes me is how calm she stayed.
entries.example_interview: What strikes me is how friendly people are here compared with my hometown.
entries.example_discussion: What strikes me is that neither student mentions the teachers' point of view.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, personal. A pseudo-cleft that foregrounds your reaction. Not "what strikes me, it is", a calque of French.

entries.definition: a cleft structure used to put strong emphasis on one part of a sentence
entries.example_academic: It is funding, not design, that explains the failure of the program.
entries.example_spoken: It is the noise that bothers me, not the heat.
entries.example_interview: It was my grandmother who taught me to cook, and it is cooking that relaxes me most.
entries.example_discussion: It is housing, rather than wages, that drives young people out of cities.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Cleft sentence: "It is/was + focus + that/who + rest". French speakers know "c'est… que" but rarely use it in English, where it adds strong emphasis.

entries.definition: used in speech to make your point sound modest or to clarify what you mean
entries.translation_fr: tout ce que je dis, c'est que
entries.example_academic: All I'm saying is that the data need checking before we publish.
entries.example_spoken: All I'm saying is, maybe we should leave earlier.
entries.example_interview: All I'm saying is that a gap year isn't a waste of time if you use it well.
entries.example_discussion: All I'm saying is that we need evidence before we ban phones in every school.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Softens a point while insisting on it. Avoid it in formal writing.

entries.definition: used to introduce the single most important point you want to make
entries.example_academic: If there is one thing the crisis showed, it is the value of local suppliers.
entries.example_spoken: If there is one thing I've learned, it's to back up my files.
entries.example_interview: If there is one thing I'm proud of, it's learning Spanish on my own.
entries.example_discussion: If there is one thing both students agree on, it is that the current system fails rural families.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Structure: "If there is one thing (that) X, it is Y". Keep both parts.

entries.definition: used to introduce the point you consider most important
entries.example_academic: What really matters is whether the changes improve patient outcomes.
entries.example_spoken: What really matters is that everyone got home safely.
entries.example_interview: What really matters is that I enjoy what I study, not just the salary.
entries.example_discussion: What really matters is not the price of the program but who can access it.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. A pseudo-cleft. "Matters" agrees with "what" (singular). Not "what really matter is".

entries.definition: used to introduce something surprising or odd
entries.example_academic: Funnily enough, the least expensive treatment turned out to be the most effective.
entries.example_spoken: Funnily enough, I was just thinking about you.
entries.example_interview: Funnily enough, I hated science at school, and now I'm studying chemistry.
entries.example_discussion: Funnily enough, the cheapest option in Kim's list is also the greenest.
entries.usage_note: Informal, British in flavor. "Oddly enough" and "strangely enough" are neutral alternatives.

entries.definition: used to introduce something surprising but true
entries.translation_fr: crois-le ou non, aussi incroyable que cela paraisse
entries.example_academic: Believe it or not, the tiny island once had a population of ten thousand.
entries.example_spoken: Believe it or not, I've never seen the sea.
entries.example_interview: Believe it or not, I learned English mostly from cooking videos.
entries.example_discussion: Believe it or not, the city spends more on parking than on libraries.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Fine in an Interview answer, too casual for an essay.

entries.definition: used to say that something happened by chance, either good or bad
entries.translation_fr: par chance, le hasard a voulu que
entries.example_academic: As luck would have it, the archive had survived the fire.
entries.example_spoken: As luck would have it, there was one seat left.
entries.example_interview: As luck would have it, my first boss was also from my hometown.
entries.example_discussion: As luck would have it, a similar policy was tried in 2015, so we have data.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Can introduce good or bad luck; context decides.

entries.definition: used in speech to add that what you just said is also true of something else
entries.example_academic: The museum has no café; come to that, it has no shop either.
entries.example_spoken: I've never been to Rome. Come to that, I've never been to Italy.
entries.example_interview: I don't really watch TV. Come to that, I don't watch many films either.
entries.example_discussion: Few students use the gym; come to that, few use the library on weekends either.
entries.usage_note: Informal, British. "For that matter" is the neutral equivalent.

entries.definition: used to offer an opinion or fact modestly, admitting it may not be important
entries.example_academic: For what it's worth, the earlier study reached the same conclusion.
entries.example_spoken: For what it's worth, I think you made the right choice.
entries.example_interview: For what it's worth, I think I'd be a good fit for this team.
entries.example_discussion: For what it's worth, my own school tried this and the results were mixed.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Modest way to add a view. Written "for what it is worth" in formal texts.

entries.definition: used to correct or limit what you have just said, or to return to the main point
entries.example_academic: The plan failed, or at any rate it did not meet its targets.
entries.example_spoken: At any rate, we'll know more tomorrow.
entries.example_interview: I loved that job, or at any rate most of it.
entries.example_discussion: At any rate, the figures do not support the claim that crime has doubled.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Two uses: correcting yourself ("or at any rate…") and moving on ("At any rate, …").

entries.definition: used to show that you are saying what you really think
entries.example_academic: In all honesty, the evidence for the second hypothesis is thin.
entries.example_spoken: In all honesty, I didn't enjoy the film.
entries.example_interview: In all honesty, I chose this major because of one inspiring teacher.
entries.example_discussion: In all honesty, I am not sure either proposal would work without more staff.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Slightly more formal than "to be honest". Not "in all frankness" in common use.

entries.definition: used to admit something you might not have said otherwise
entries.example_academic: Truth be told, the first prototype barely worked.
entries.example_spoken: Truth be told, I was a bit nervous.
entries.example_interview: Truth be told, I almost didn't apply because I thought I had no chance.
entries.example_discussion: Truth be told, the original plan never had enough funding.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. An admission. Not "to tell the truth be told", a mix of two expressions.

entries.definition: used to say that something unpleasant must be accepted as true
entries.example_academic: Let's face it: no single policy will solve the housing crisis.
entries.example_spoken: Let's face it, we're not going to finish tonight.
entries.example_interview: Let's face it, nobody enjoys exams, but they push me to really learn.
entries.example_discussion: Let's face it: most people will not change their habits unless it saves them money.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Direct; use it once per answer at most.

entries.definition: used to say that the reality is much stronger than the words you are using
entries.translation_fr: c'est le moins qu'on puisse dire
entries.example_academic: The early results were, to put it mildly, disappointing.
entries.example_spoken: The trip was, to put it mildly, a disaster.
entries.example_interview: My first attempt at cooking for friends was, to put it mildly, not a success.
entries.example_discussion: The proposal is, to put it mildly, optimistic about how quickly people will change.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, ironic. "To say the least" is a close equivalent.

entries.definition: if a situation becomes difficult and action is really necessary
entries.translation_fr: en cas de besoin, au pire
entries.example_academic: If push comes to shove, the council could sell the building.
entries.example_spoken: If push comes to shove, I can sleep on the sofa.
entries.example_interview: If push comes to shove, I could finish my degree part time while working.
entries.example_discussion: If push comes to shove, schools could share specialist teachers between sites.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Introduces a fallback option.

entries.definition: used to say that something is so obvious that it hardly needs to be said
entries.example_academic: It goes without saying that the results must be replicated.
entries.example_spoken: It goes without saying that you're welcome to stay.
entries.example_interview: It goes without saying that I'd be willing to travel for this job.
entries.example_discussion: It goes without saying that teachers must be consulted, yet none of the posts mention them.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Exact equivalent of "il va sans dire". Usually followed by "that".

entries.headword: the long and the short of it
entries.definition: the basic facts of a situation, without the details
entries.example_academic: The long and the short of it is that the project ran out of money.
entries.example_spoken: The long and the short of it is, we're moving.
entries.ipa: /ðə lɔːŋ ənd ðə ʃɔːrt ʌv ɪt/
entries.example_interview: The long and the short of it is that I fell in love with teaching during my internship.
entries.example_discussion: The long and the short of it is that Kim's plan helps only students who already own cars.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Usually "The long and the short of it is (that)…".

entries.headword: off the top of my head
entries.definition: without checking or thinking carefully; from memory
entries.translation_fr: de mémoire, comme ça sans réfléchir
entries.example_academic: Off the top of my head, I'd estimate the sample at about two hundred.
entries.example_spoken: Off the top of my head, I can't remember her name.
entries.example_interview: Off the top of my head, I'd say my biggest strength is patience.
entries.example_discussion: Off the top of my head, I can think of three cities where this approach has worked.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Signals an approximate answer. Very useful in Interview when you need time.

entries.definition: used to state something clearly and officially, so that it is known
entries.translation_fr: pour mémoire, pour qu'on le sache
entries.example_academic: For the record, the committee did not approve the final version.
entries.example_spoken: For the record, I never said that.
entries.example_interview: For the record, I wasn't the one who broke the printer.
entries.example_discussion: For the record, my point was about cost, not about whether the program is useful.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Clarifies your position. Not "for the memory".

entries.definition: used to add a detail that supports or surprisingly corrects what was said
entries.example_academic: As a matter of fact, the first recorded use of the term is much older.
entries.example_spoken: As a matter of fact, I've just finished it.
entries.example_interview: As a matter of fact, I've already started learning the software this job uses.
entries.example_discussion: As a matter of fact, the city tried a similar ban in 2012.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often introduces a surprising detail. "Actually" is the shorter equivalent.

entries.definition: used to say that someone's remark has made you notice or remember something
entries.example_academic: Now that you mention it, the second graph does look odd.
entries.example_spoken: Now that you mention it, I haven't seen her for weeks.
entries.example_interview: Now that you mention it, my interest in design probably started with Lego.
entries.example_discussion: Now that you mention it, Jonah, the survey did leave out evening students.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Reacts to someone else's remark.

entries.definition: used to introduce a topic connected to what was just mentioned
entries.translation_fr: à ce propos, en parlant de ça
entries.example_academic: Speaking of which, the next conference will focus on this very issue.
entries.example_spoken: Speaking of which, have you booked the tickets?
entries.example_interview: I love hiking. Speaking of which, I'm planning a trip to the Alps this summer.
entries.example_discussion: Several students mentioned costs. Speaking of which, nobody has asked who would pay for maintenance.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Links to the previous topic naturally.

entries.definition: used to say that you have changed your mind after thinking again
entries.example_academic: On second thought, a smaller pilot study might be wiser.
entries.example_spoken: On second thought, I'll stay home.
entries.example_interview: I wanted to study law, but on second thought, I realized I preferred working with data.
entries.example_discussion: On second thought, I agree with Mia that a gradual approach would be safer.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. American form; British English says "on second thoughts".

entries.definition: used to say that you think you remember correctly
entries.example_academic: If memory serves, the law was passed in 1994.
entries.example_spoken: If memory serves, she lives near the station.
entries.example_interview: If memory serves, I was about eight when I first went abroad.
entries.example_discussion: If memory serves, a similar policy was rejected by voters a few years ago.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, slightly literary. "If memory serves me right" is also common.

entries.definition: in my opinion
entries.example_academic: To my mind, the strongest evidence comes from the field studies.
entries.example_spoken: To my mind, it's the best café in town.
entries.example_interview: To my mind, a good teacher is someone who makes you curious.
entries.example_discussion: To my mind, the professor's question has no single answer, which is why the debate matters.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. A natural alternative to "in my opinion". Not "for my mind".

entries.definition: used in speech to point out the important issue or problem
entries.example_academic: That's the thing: nobody knows how long the effect lasts.
entries.example_spoken: That's the thing, I don't have a car.
entries.example_interview: I'd love to travel more, but that's the thing, I can't afford it yet.
entries.example_discussion: That's the thing: a ban does nothing if it is never enforced.
entries.usage_note: Informal, spoken. Signals the crux of the matter. Avoid in formal essays.

entries.definition: used in speech to reject one possible explanation before giving the real one
entries.example_academic: It's not that the theory is wrong; it simply explains too little.
entries.example_spoken: It's not that I don't like him. I just don't know him.
entries.example_interview: It's not that I dislike big cities; I just sleep better in quiet places.
entries.example_discussion: It's not that Daniel is wrong; it's just that he answers a different question.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Usually followed by a second clause with "just" or "simply". Equivalent of "ce n'est pas que…".
